title: The self no weapon can cut
hookLine: Krishna's first real teaching is about who is actually standing on the field, and it starts with clothes
carry: the atman is never born, never dies
last: THE TEACHING BEGINS WHEN YOU ASK: TEACH ME.

lines: A PHOTO OF YOU AT FIVE.
cards: Find a photo of yourself at five. Much of that little body has been rebuilt since. The face, the voice, the height, what you're afraid of, what you love.
And yet you point at it and say: that's me. Something was there at five, and at fifteen, and is here right now, listening. What is it?
Arjuna is grieving for the people on the field. Krishna's first move is to ask who, exactly, is on the field.

teach.h: THE WISE DON'T GRIEVE THE LIVING OR DEAD.
teach.b: You grieve for those who shouldn't be grieved for, Krishna says, and yet you speak like someone wise. The wise don't grieve for the living or the dead.
There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings, and there will never be a time when we cease to be. Then the picture from your photo.
Just as the one who lives in this body passes through childhood, youth and old age, it passes on to another body. The wise aren't confused by it. Cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go.
Bear them. What lasts, Krishna says, is the self, the atman, the one who lives in the body. In Sanskrit: na jayate mriyate va kadachin.
It is not born, it does not die, at any time.
Edwin Arnold, in 1885, turned it into verse: "Never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never; Never was time it was not; End and Beginning are dreams!" Then the everyday picture.
As a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the self throws off worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. Nainam chhindanti shastrani, nainam dahati pavakah. Weapons don't cut it.

teach.h: WEAPONS DON'T CUT IT. FIRE DOESN'T BURN IT.
teach.b: Fire doesn't burn it. Water doesn't wet it. Wind doesn't dry it.
Hindu schools read this differently. Some hear one Self in everyone. Others hear many eternal selves, pointing to that line: nor you, nor these kings.
Readers have also long wrestled with the fact that it's said on a battlefield. But its first job is plain: to tell a grieving man that what he loves in them is not what arrows reach.
This is the atman, and it's why so many Hindu families hear these verses at a funeral.

how: Gita 2.20 and 2.22–2.23, on the self that is never born and never dies, are often recited at Hindu funerals and in times of grief.

o: a ghost that lingers after death
the self that lives in the body
the stars that rule your fate

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: the self, the one who lives in the body
bodies thrown off for new ones
it is not born, it does not die
they come and go; bear them

s: Krishna starts by telling Arjuna the enemy deserves to die
he starts with who is really on the field: the self that is never born and never dies.
the Gita compares bodies to worn-out clothes
as a person puts on new clothes, the self takes on new bodies.
all Hindu schools read these verses the same way
some hear one Self in everyone; others hear many eternal selves, from 'nor you, nor these kings'.

games.q: you're Krishna. your friend is weeping over the people on the field. what's the first thing you teach him?
o: who is really on the field: the self that isn't slain.
you'll feel better after the battle.
games.why: he teaches the self first: never born, never dies, and no weapon reaches it. the wise don't grieve for the living or the dead.

practice: Notice a sensation, the chair under you, then a thought, then a feeling, and watch each one come and go.
Then, gently, notice what's noticing, the thing that was there at five and is here now, and rest as it for a few breaths without grabbing or naming it.
In the Gita's picture, heat and cold, pleasure and pain keep passing through, and the one watching them doesn't come and go.

wordCard.voice: Atman. The self, the one who lives in the body: never born, never dies, and no weapon reaches it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the self. in the Gita, the one who lives in the body and is not slain when the body is.

carryVoice: Your line: the atman is never born, never dies. Old clothes, same wearer. That's day one hundred sixty-two.
